lead.t: | Arterial blood gas (ABG) | Is there hypoxaemia or hypercapnia indicating respiratory failure? | PaO₂ < 60 mmHg or PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg in chronic bronchitis suggests advanced disease; normal ABG in mild acute bronchitis. |

b: Failure of gas exchange: PaO2 under 8 kPa (60 mmHg) with or without a raised PaCO2 over 6.5 kPa (50 mmHg).

Mechanisms of hypoxaemia (type I): (1) low inspired oxygen partial pressure (altitude), (2) alveolar hypoventilation, (3) diffusion impairment, (4) ventilation-perfusion mismatch (the commonest) , (5) right-to-left shunt (does not correct w

Post-operative respiratory failure: atelectasis (the commonest cause of early post-operative fever and hypoxia), pneumonia, pulmonary oedema (fluid overload), pulmonary embolism, residual anaesthetic or opioid effects, splinting from pain,

Treatment: treat the cause; oxygen (titrated: 88 to 92% target in type II, over 94% in type I); physiotherapy, analgesia and incentive spirometry; non-invasive ventilation (CPAP or BiPAP) ; intubation and mechanical ventilation if failing.

qs.q: A 25-year-old male is admitted with a cervical spine fracture. Which of the following injury levels would result in fatal respiratory failure without immediate mechanical ventilation due to involvement of the phrenic nerve?
qs.e: The phrenic nerve arises from C3 to C5, meaning injuries above C3 are fatal without ventilation. C1 to C2 injuries are well above this critical threshold.
qs.s: Spinal Cord Injury: Assessment, Spinal Shock and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman with severe kyphoscoliosis presents with acute-on-chronic respiratory failure, displaying a low PaO2 and an elevated PaCO2. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism responsible for her hypercapnia?
qs.e: Alveolar hypoventilation is the sole mechanism responsible for Type II hypercapnic respiratory failure, which is seen in chest wall abnormalities like kyphoscoliosis. V/Q mismatch and shunts are the primary mechanisms for Type I hypoxaemic respiratory failure.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 60-year-old man with neuromuscular disease presents with acute ventilatory failure. His arterial blood gas reveals a PaO2 of 7 kPa and a PaCO2 of 7.2 kPa. What is the classification and fundamental abnormality of his respiratory failure?
o: Type I failure caused by ventilation-perfusion mismatch
Type II failure caused by increased metabolic carbon dioxide production
Type I failure caused by right-to-left pulmonary shunt
Type II failure caused by alveolar hypoventilation
qs.e: A PaO2 under 8 kPa combined with a PaCO2 over 6.5 kPa defines Type II respiratory failure, which is fundamentally caused by alveolar hypoventilation. Neuromuscular diseases cause hypoventilation rather than primary V/Q mismatch or shunt.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old man undergoes emergency laparotomy for a perforated peptic ulcer and develops acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. On the third day, he is positioned face-down for 16 hours a day. What is the primary physiological rationale for this specific intervention in moderate to severe ARDS?
o: Reduction of intra-abdominal pressure on the diaphragm
Minimisation of barotrauma via lowered peak airway pressures
Direct drainage of posterior alveolar fluid collections
qs.e: Prone positioning improves ventilation-perfusion matching by recruiting dorsal lung units while ventral perfusion remains well-maintained. It does not directly drain fluid collections or alter intra-abdominal pressure as its primary mechanism.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old male is admitted with respiratory failure and descending paralysis following a mamba bite. Aside from mechanical ventilation, which adjunctive pharmacological therapy can be given as a trial for post-synaptic neurotoxins?
qs.e: An anticholinesterase trial using neostigmine with atropine is used for post-synaptic neurotoxin-induced paralysis. Adrenaline is used for anaphylactic reactions to antivenom.
qs.s: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections, and Snake Bites: MCQs

qs.q: A polytrauma patient requires a definitive airway due to a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7 and impending respiratory failure. Which technique represents the standard method for establishing this airway while protecting the cervical spine?
o: Insertion of an oropharyngeal Guedel airway alone
Surgical cricothyroidotomy as the primary choice
Orotracheal intubation using rapid sequence induction
qs.e: A definitive airway is established via orotracheal intubation using rapid sequence induction combined with manual in-line stabilisation. Surgical cricothyroidotomy is reserved for when intubation fails or is impossible due to severe facial or laryngeal trauma.
qs.s: Trauma Management: ATLS Primary Survey, Resuscitation and Abdominal: MCQs

qs.q: A patient develops severe sepsis followed by progressive respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Histopathological analysis of the lungs shows prominent hyaline membrane formation lining alveolar walls, alveolar septal oedema, and type II pneumocyte hyperplasia. Which phase of diffuse alveolar damage is characterized by hyaline membranes?
qs.e: The exudative phase of diffuse alveolar damage (ARDS) occurs from days 1 to 7 and is characterized by hyaline membranes and alveolar oedema. Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia and organization predominate in the subsequent proliferative phase.
qs.s: Essential Cardiovascular Pathology: Atherosclerosis to Endoc: MCQs

qs.q: A 60-year-old patient who survived severe acute pancreatitis develops progressive hypoxaemia and respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Post-mortem histological examination of the lungs reveals protein-rich hyaline membranes lining the alveolar walls alongside interstitial oedema. Which phase of diffuse alveolar damage is this patient most likely in?
qs.e: The exudative phase of diffuse alveolar damage (ARDS) occurs during days 1 to 7 and is characterized by hyaline membrane formation and alveolar septal oedema. The proliferative and fibrotic phases occur later in the disease timeline.

es.q: List and explain the physiological differences and common causes associated with Type I and Type II respiratory failure.
es.m:
- **Definition:** Failure of gas exchange defined by PaO2 under 8 kPa (60 mmHg), with or without raised PaCO2 over 6.5 kPa (50 mmHg).
- **Type I blood gas and mechanism:** Low PaO2 with normal or low PaCO2, caused by V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion impairment, low inspired oxygen, or alveolar hypoventilation.
- **Type I causes:** Collapse (atelectasis), consolidation (pneumonia), pulmonary contusion, pulmonary oedema, pulmonary embolus, and ARDS.
- **Type II blood gas and mechanism:** Low PaO2 with a high PaCO2, caused by alveolar hypoventilation.
- **Type II causes:** COPD, chest trauma (flail chest), respiratory depression (opioids, sedatives), raised ICP, spinal cord lesions, and neuromusc

es.q: Discuss the principles of intensive care unit (ICU) and high-dependency unit (HDU) care, detailing severity triggers, admission factors, respiratory failure classification, oxygen delivery, and blood gas interpretation.
es.m:
- **ICU function:** Provides mechanical support of failing organs with continuous monitoring and usually 1:1 nursing across respiratory, renal, cardiac, hepatic, and neurological systems.
- **HDU function:** Provides close monitoring for unstable, non-organ-failing patients with a patient-to-nurse ratio of at least 2:1 as a step-down from ICU.
- **ICU admission triggers (airway and breathing):** Threatened airway, respiratory arrest, respiratory rate over 40 or under 8 per minute, and oxygen saturation under 90% on over 50% oxygen.
- **ICU admission triggers (circulation and neurology):** Cardiac arrest, pulse under 40 or over 140 per minute, systolic blood pressure under 90 mmHg, sudden dro

es.q: Acute Lung Injury (ALI) and Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) represent a spectrum of severe respiratory failure. a) Define Acute Lung Injury (ALI) and describe its clinical triad. (4 marks) b) Explain how ALI can progress to Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), highlighting the key
es.m: a) Acute Lung Injury (ALI) is characterized by an acute onset of dyspnea, decreased arterial oxygen pressure (hypoxemia), and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiograph. These infiltrates represent noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, meaning the edema is not primarily due to left-sided heart failure. (4 marks) b) ALI can progress to Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), which signifies a more severe manifestation involving diffuse alveolar capillary AND epithelial damage. ARDS presents with rapid-onset respiratory insufficiency, cyanosis, and severe arterial hypoxemia that is refractory to oxygen therapy, often leading to multisystem organ failure. ARDS is distinct from neonatal R

es.q: A critically ill patient develops acute respiratory failure refractory to oxygen therapy, with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray, in the absence of primary cardiac failure. Describe the hallmark microscopic finding characteristic of the acute phase of this condition (ARDS), and briefly
es.m: The hallmark microscopic finding characteristic of the acute phase of ARDS (Diffuse Alveolar Damage) is the presence of **hyaline membranes** lining the alveolar ducts and alveoli (2 marks). The initial cellular events in its pathogenesis involve an insult that triggers pulmonary macrophages to release **IL-8** (1 mark), leading to neutrophil chemotaxis into the alveolar space (1 mark). These activated neutrophils then release damaging oxidants and proteases (1 mark).

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Respiratory failure is the inability of the lungs to maintain adequate oxygenation or CO₂ elimination. It is classified by gas abnormalities and severity, and requires rapid identification of cause and supportive care.

sections.p: Respiratory failure occurs when PaO₂ < 60 mmHg (hypoxemic) or PaCO₂ > 50 mmHg with pH < 7.35 (hypercapnic) despite maximal effort. Diagnosis uses arterial blood gas (ABG) and clinical assessment of work of breathing.
b: ABG provides the primary objective criteria.
Look for tachypnea, accessory‑muscle use, altered mental status.

sections.p: The American Thoracic Society grades failure as mild, moderate, or severe based on PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio and PaCO₂ levels. This guides urgency of ventilatory support.
b: Mild: PaO₂ 60‑80 mmHg, PaCO₂ ≤45 mmHg.
Moderate: PaO₂ 40‑60 mmHg or PaCO₂ 45‑60 mmHg.
Severe: PaO₂ <40 mmHg or PaCO₂ >60 mmHg with acidosis.

sections.p: Identify whether the primary problem is hypoxemic (type 1) or hypercapnic (type 2) and then consider common etiologies, especially those seen in low‑resource settings.
b: Type 1: pneumonia, TB, pulmonary embolism, ARDS, severe malaria.
Type 2: COPD exacerbation, asthma status, neuromuscular weakness (GBS, myasthenia), chest wall trauma.
Mixed: sepsis with multi‑organ failure, severe anemia, high‑altitude exposure.

sections.p: Patients develop dyspnea, tachypnea, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, altered consciousness, and may have a paradoxical rise in PaCO₂ indicating fatigue.
b: Acute: rapid onset, often after infection or asthma attack.
Chronic: progressive dyspnea, weight loss, nocturnal hypoventilation.

sections.p: Targeted tests answer specific questions about gas exchange, underlying disease, and severity.

t.b: What are the oxygenation and ventilation status? Shows PaO₂, PaCO₂, pH; guides need for ventilation.
What structural lung pathology is present? Detects pneumonia, effusion, pneumothorax, infiltrates.
Is oxygen saturation adequate? Quick bedside screen; if unavailable, use clinical signs.
Is there obstructive airflow limitation? Helps differentiate COPD/asthma from neuromuscular causes.
Is infection or hemolysis contributing? Guides antimicrobial therapy in endemic areas.

sections.p: Recognize signs that herald rapid deterioration and life‑threatening sequelae.
b: Rising PaCO₂ or falling pH despite increased effort.
Severe hypoxemia (SpO₂ < 85%) or hemodynamic instability.
Altered mental status, bradycardia, or impending cardiac arrest.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide ventilatory support and monitor closely. Choose therapies based on pathophysiology and resource availability.
b: Oxygen therapy: titrate to SpO₂ 92‑96% (88‑92% in COPD).
Non‑invasive ventilation (BiPAP) for hypercapnic failure if conscious.
Intubation and mechanical ventilation for severe hypoxemia or exhaustion.
Bronchodilators and steroids for asthma/ COPD exacerbations.
Antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia, anti‑TB drugs for TB, antimalarials for malaria.
Sodium bicarbonate only if metabolic acidosis coexists; not for pure respiratory acidosis.

sections.p: After acute stabilization, address chronic risk factors and arrange monitoring to avoid recurrence.
b: Vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal).
Smoking cessation, pulmonary rehabilitation.
Long‑term oxygen for chronic hypoxemia.
Regular review of ventilatory settings and adherence to therapy.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic respiratory failure but have different primary mechanisms.
b: Cardiac failure – presents with dyspnea but primary problem is fluid overload.
Anemia – low oxygen content without gas exchange abnormality.
Severe sepsis – may cause hypoxia but primary driver is circulatory shock.

sections.p: Beware of values that appear normal despite serious pathology.
b: Normal PaCO₂ in a pregnant patient is abnormal (physiologic PaCO₂ is lower).
Pulse oximetry may be falsely high in carbon monoxide poisoning.
ABG may show normal PaO₂ if supplemental O₂ is already given, masking underlying lung disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden inability to speak full sentences, cyanosis, or unresponsive patient.
Rapidly rising PaCO₂ (>55 mmHg) or falling pH (<7.30) despite maximal effort.

faq.q: Why does PaCO₂ rise in a patient who looks very breathless?
faq.a: It indicates respiratory muscle fatigue; the patient can no longer increase ventilation.

faq.q: When is non‑invasive ventilation preferred over intubation?
faq.a: When the patient is alert, can protect the airway, and has hypercapnic failure without severe hypoxemia.

faq.q: Can a normal chest X‑ray rule out respiratory failure?
faq.a: No; gas exchange abnormalities can exist with a normal radiograph, especially early in COPD or neuromuscular weakness.
